{{short description|American physicist}}
[[File:330-PSA-153-63 (USN 711326) (22171848378) (cropped).jpg|thumb|Robert Fischell in 1963]]
'''Robert Fischell''' (born February 10, 1929) is a physicist, [[List of prolific inventors|prolific inventor]], and holder of more than 200 U.S. and foreign medical patents.<ref>{{cite book |title=Who's who in America |date=2003 |publisher=Marquis Who's Who |page=1613 |isbn=9780837969756 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fxsRzGxzcowC |access-date=20 August 2021}}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20030825071413/http://web.mit.edu/invent/iow/fischell.html MIT Inventor of the Week Archives.] Accessed February 22, 2007.</ref><ref>[http://www.nationalhealthmuseum.org/news/articles/newest_trustees.html "NHM Board Welcomes Renowned Health and Medical Figures as Newest Trustees,"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120206080417/http://www.nationalhealthmuseum.org/news/articles/newest_trustees.html |date=2012-02-06 }} ''National Health Museum News'', Accessed February 22, 2007.</ref><ref name="MDDI_Fischell">[http://www.devicelink.com/mddi/archive/04/08/039.html "Industry Pioneer – Robert Fischell,"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040907190836/http://www.devicelink.com/mddi/archive/04/08/039.html |date=2004-09-07 }} ''Medical Device & Diagnostic Industry – August 2004''. Accessed February 22, 2007.</ref><ref>[http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&u=%2Fnetahtml%2FPTO%2Fsearch-adv.htm&r=0&p=1&f=S&l=50&d=PTXT&Query=apt%2F1+and+in%2Ffischell-robert$ US Patents of Robert E. Fischell]</ref> His inventions have led to the creation of several [[biotechnology]] companies. He worked at the [[Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory]] full-time for 25 years and part-time for an additional 13 years. He contributed to APL's satellite navigation work; he later developed a rechargeable implantable pacemaker that could be programmed with radiowaves,<ref>Love JW, Lewis KB, Fischell RE, [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/query.fcgi?cmd=Retrieve&db=PubMed&list_uids=1099261&dopt=Abstract "The Johns Hopkins rechargeable pacemaker. Historical aspect."] ''JAMA'' 1975 Oct 6;234(1):64-6.</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/19970618060707/http://www.sti.nasa.gov/tto/spinoff1996/25.html "Programmable Pacemaker,"] ''Spinoff (Publication of NASA featuring commercial applications of space technology)'', 1996. Accessed February 25, 2007.</ref><ref>Fischell R. (1998), [http://techdigest.jhuapl.edu/td1901/fischell.pdf "Applications of Transit Satellite Technology to Biomedical Devices,"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902230524/http://techdigest.jhuapl.edu/td1901/fischell.pdf |date=2006-09-02 }} ''Johns Hopkins APL Technical Digest''; Vol 19, No. 1.</ref><ref>[http://www.aemf.org/page.php?id=40 "The Alfred Mann Foundation,"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070218174402/http://www.aemf.org/page.php?id=40 |date=2007-02-18 }} ''Mission and History'', Accessed February 25, 2007.</ref> ([[Pacesetter Systems]] purchased by Siemens, now the CRM division of [[St. Jude Medical]]). He and his team at Hopkins also helped miniaturize the [[Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator|implantable cardiac defibrillator]].<ref name="Discover_Fischell">Neal E. (2003), [http://discovermagazine.com/2003/nov/technology-for-humanity/ "Technology for Humanity: Robert Fischell,"] ''Discover Magazine'', Vol. 24, No. 11.</ref> Mr. Fischell went on to invent the implantable [[insulin pump]] ([[MiniMed]], spun off from [[Pacesetter Systems]] in 1985), numerous coronary [[stent]]s used to open clogged arteries (IsoStent merged with [[Cordis (medical)|Cordis]], in turn purchased by [[Johnson & Johnson]]),<ref>[http://www.prnewswire.com/cgi-bin/stories.pl?ACCT=104&STORY=/www/story/2-11-98/413707&EDATE= "Cordis Acquires IsoStent Technology; Continues Collaborative Radioactive Stent Research,"] ''PRNewswire'', Accessed February 22, 2007.</ref> and two feedback systems that provide early warning of [[epileptic seizure]]s (NeuroPace) and [[heart attacks]] (Angel Medical Systems).<ref name="MDDI_Fischell" /> Fischell recently donated $30 million to the University of Maryland College Park Foundation to establish a bioengineering department and an institute for biomedical devices at the [[A. James Clark School of Engineering]].<ref>[http://www.eng.umd.edu/spotlight/fischell/ The Fischell Department of Bioengineering and the Robert E. Fischell Institute for Biomedical Devices.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100601165934/http://www.eng.umd.edu/spotlight/fischell/ |date=2010-06-01 }} Accessed February 22, 2007.</ref>

In 2005, he was awarded the [[TED (conference)|TED]] Prize, receiving $100,000 and three wishes, including a braintrust on medical liability and the successful design of a device to cure [[migraine]]s.<ref>[http://www.tedprize.org/2005-winners/#rfischell 2005 Winners] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081221135816/http://www.tedprize.org/2005-winners/ |date=2008-12-21 }} tedprize.org, accessed 09-08-2012</ref>

Fischell received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in [[mechanical engineering]] from [[Duke University]] in 1951, where he became a brother of [[Zeta Beta Tau]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://zbt.org/about-zbt/notable-brothers/|publisher=[[Zeta Beta Tau]]|title= Notable Brothers|language=en-US|url-status=live|archive-date=September 30, 2025|archive-url=https://archive.today/20250930060311/https://zbt.org/about-zbt/notable-brothers/}}</ref> He received his [[Master of Science|M.S.]] from the [[University of Maryland]] in 1953 in [[physics]], which is part of the [[University of Maryland College of Computer, Mathematical, and Natural Sciences]]. Fischell was awarded an [[honorary degree|honorary doctorate]] from the [[University of Maryland]] in 1996.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.angel-med.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=3:robert-e-fischell&catid=2:management&Itemid=11|title = Angel Medical Systems – It's about time}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bioe.umd.edu/about/meetthefischells.html |title=Bioengineering, University of Maryland |accessdate=2010-05-08 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100531185800/http://www.bioe.umd.edu/about/meetthefischells.html |archivedate=2010-05-31 }}</ref>

He has three sons (from oldest to youngest), David, Tim, and Scott Fischell. He is married to Susan R. Fischell, and they live in Maryland.

He was awarded the [[National Medal of Technology and Innovation]] in 2016.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fischell to Receive National Medal of Technology and Innovation|url=http://www.eng.umd.edu/html/news/news_story.php?id=9495|publisher=University of Maryland|accessdate=5 January 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://nationalmedals.org/laureates |title = Laureates - National Science and Technology Medals Foundation}}</ref>
